{{Short description|None}}
{{see also|List of Native American politicians}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=April 2025}}
[[File:Native Americans in US House.svg|thumb|Map of all three [[Congressional district#United States|congressional districts]] represented by Native Americans at the beginning of the [[119th United States Congress|119th Congress]]. At the time, one of [[Oklahoma]]'s two senators also was a Native American.]]

This is a list of [[Native Americans in the United States|Native Americans]] with documented tribal ancestry or affiliation who are in the [[United States Congress]]. All entries on this list are related to Native American tribes based in the [[continental United States]]. There are [[Native Hawaiians]] who [[List of Asian Americans and Pacific Islands Americans in the United States Congress|have served in Congress]], but they are not listed here because they are distinct from North American Natives. [[Richard H. Cain]] was the first Native American to serve in Congress, serving in the [[United States House of Representatives]]. [[Charles Curtis]] was the first Native American to serve in the [[United States Senate]] and would go on to become the first Native American [[Vice President of the United States]].

Only two Native Americans served in the [[115th United States Congress|115th Congress]]: [[Tom Cole]] (serving since 2003) and [[Markwayne Mullin]] (served from 2013 until 2023), both of whom are Republican Representatives from Oklahoma. On [[2018 United States House of Representatives elections|November 6, 2018]], Democrats [[Sharice Davids]] of Kansas and [[Deb Haaland]] of New Mexico were elected to the U.S. House of Representatives, and the [[116th United States Congress|116th Congress]], which commenced on January 3, 2019, had four Native Americans. Davids and Haaland are the first two Native American women with documented tribal ancestry to serve in Congress. At the start of the [[117th United States Congress|117th Congress]] on January 3, 2021, five Native Americans were serving in the House, the largest Native delegation in history: Cole, Mullin, Haaland and Davids were all reelected in 2020, with Republican [[Yvette Herrell]] of New Mexico elected for the first time in 2020. The number dropped back down to four on March 16, 2021 when Haaland resigned her House seat to become the first Native American [[United States Secretary of the Interior|Secretary of the Interior]].

On [[2022 Alaska's at-large congressional district special election|August 16, 2022]], [[Mary Peltola]], a [[Yup'ik]] woman, was elected to the U.S. House of Representatives to represent Alaska, becoming the first person with documented [[Alaska Natives|Native Alaskan]] ancestry to serve in Congress. This returned the number of the Native delegation to five, with a partisan split of three Republicans and two Democrats. This also marked the first time that a Native American, Native Alaskan, and Native Hawaiian ([[Kai Kahele]]) simultaneously served in Congress.

Following the [[2022 United States House of Representatives elections|November 2022 elections]], incumbents Cole (R-OK), Davids (D-KS) and Peltola (D-AK) all retained their seats, while Cherokee Republican Markwayne Mullin retired from the House and was elected to the Senate: Mullin became the first Native senator since the retirement of [[Ben Nighthorse Campbell]] (R-CO) in 2005, and his House seat was won by Choctaw Republican [[Josh Brecheen]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Native candidates headed for Congress after midterms |date=November 10, 2022 |url=https://www.cherokeephoenix.org/news/native-candidates-headed-for-congress-after-midterms/article_94e41744-6121-11ed-927c-5b621e875960.html |publisher=[[Cherokee Phoenix]] |accessdate=November 10, 2022}}</ref> In the same election, Yvette Herrell lost her seat due to redistricting, which drew litigation over alleged political [[gerrymandering]];<ref>{{cite web |date=2023-01-09 |title=New Mexico Supreme Court considers gerrymandering question |url=https://www.krqe.com/news/politics-government/new-mexico-supreme-court-considers-gerrymandering-question/ |access-date=2023-02-13 |website=KRQE NEWS 13 - Breaking News, Albuquerque News, New Mexico News, Weather, and Videos |language=en-US}}</ref> as such, Native Americans in the [[118th Congress]] remained five, four in the House and one in the Senate. The partisan split is three Republicans and two Democrats. The states represented by Native members of Congress also dropped from four to three with Herrell's defeat in New Mexico.

Following the [[2024 United States House of Representatives elections|November 2024 elections]], incumbents Brecheen (R-OK), Cole (R-OK), and Davids (D-KS) retained their seats, while Peltola (D-AK) [[2024 United States House of Representatives election in Alaska|lost re-election]]. As such, Native Americans in the [[119th Congress]] went down to four, three in the House and one in the Senate. The partisan split is three Republicans and one Democrat.
